pages.title: Title
pages.summary: Title slide: Background, Statistics & Portfolio Theory — from returns and probability distributions to mean–variance analysis and the CAPM.

pages.title: What this deck covers
pages.summary: TOC: expected utility & stochastic dominance; returns, random variables & distributions; portfolio mathematics; distribution of stock returns; mean–variance analysis; efficient set mathematics; practice & estimation risk (Jorion 1992); the CAPM.

pages.title: Expected utility theory
pages.summary: vNM representation theorem: completeness, transitivity, continuity, independence imply a utility u with A ⪰ B ⟺ E[u(X_A)] ≥ E[u(X_B)]. Investors maximize expected utility of wealth, not expected wealth. u unique up to positive affine transformation. MV analysis is exact under quadratic u or jointly normal returns.

pages.title: Risk aversion lives in the curvature of u
pages.summary: Concave u ⟺ dislikes a fair gamble. Figure: chord below curve, E[u(W)] < u(E[W]), CE and risk premium π marked. Risk averse u''<0, neutral linear, loving u''>0. Jensen's inequality. Arrow–Pratt A(W) = −u''(W)/u'(W).

pages.title: Certainty equivalent and risk premium
pages.summary: u(CE)=E[u(W)]; π = E[W] − CE ≥ 0. Pratt approximation π ≈ ½A(W)σ² for small fair gambles. Utility families: quadratic W − (b/2)W², CRRA W^(1−γ)/(1−γ), CARA −e^(−αW), log ln W (CRRA γ=1, Kelly). MV works if u quadratic or returns jointly normal.

pages.title: First-order stochastic dominance (FSD)
pages.summary: A FSD B if F_A(r) ≤ F_B(r) for all r (strict somewhere) — CDF shifted right. Equivalent: E[u(r_A)] ≥ E[u(r_B)] for every non-decreasing u; r_A =d r_B + η with η ≥ 0. Unanimity rule for everyone preferring more to less.

pages.title: Second-order stochastic dominance (SSD)
pages.summary: A SSD B if ∫_{−∞}^{r}[F_B − F_A] dt ≥ 0 for all r. Equivalent: E[u(r_A)] ≥ E[u(r_B)] for every non-decreasing concave u; B = A + worsening shift + mean-preserving spread. Two normals with the same mean: A SSD B ⟺ σ²_A ≤ σ²_B. CDFs cross at common mean.

pages.title: Random variables
pages.summary: Notation: tilde = random variable; E, σ², σ; density p(x); probabilities p_i; sample x̄, s²; weights w_j; σ_xy, ρ_xy. First two moments do most of the work.

pages.title: Mean and variance
pages.summary: Discrete: E(X)=Σp_iX_i; σ²=Σp_i(X_i−E)². Continuous: same with integrals. σ = √σ².

pages.title: Why we lean on the normal
pages.summary: Normal fully characterized by mean and variance. P(±1σ)=0.6826, P(±2σ)=0.9550. Standardization r=(x−E)/σ ~ N(0,1). Returns normal ⟹ (E, σ) pin down everything ⟹ MV is the right framework, not a simplification. Bell-curve figure with shaded bands.

pages.title: Sample mean and sample variance
pages.summary: x̄ = (1/T)Σx_t; s² = (1/(T−1))Σ(x_t−x̄)² (unbiased, df correction). SE(x̄)=σ/√T; SE(s²)≈σ²√(2/(T−1)). Convergence 1/√T: doubling precision quadruples the sample. Sample statistics are themselves random.

pages.title: Testing for normality
pages.summary: Studentized range SR=(max−min)/s; skewness (3rd standardized moment, equities typically negative); kurtosis (4th; normal = 3, daily returns much higher). Fama (1965): a 4σ daily return should occur once in 50 years under normality; in data roughly four times every five years.

pages.title: From price changes to returns
pages.summary: Multi-period returns compound: 1+R = Π(1+r_t); logs convert product to sum. Convention: cross-section — simple returns normal (portfolios are sums); time-series — log returns i.i.d. normal ⟹ simple returns lognormal; lognormal rules out negative prices.

pages.title: Mean and variance of a lognormal return
pages.summary: If ln(1+r) ~ N(μ, σ²): E[r]=exp(μ+σ²/2)−1; Var(r)=exp(2μ+σ²)(exp(σ²)−1). Multivariate normal density for N×1 return vector; joint normality iff every linear combination normal; zero covariance ⟹ independence (unique to joint normal).

pages.title: Portfolio weights and the portfolio return
pages.summary: w_j = $ in stock j / $ portfolio; Σw_j = 1 (1ᵀW=1). Portfolio return R_p = Σ w_j r_j = WᵀR. Under MVN only means and (co)variances matter.

pages.title: From individual moments to portfolio moments
pages.summary: E[R_p]=Σw_jE[r_j]=Wᵀμ. Two-asset variance σ²_p = w₁²σ₁² + w₂²σ₂² + 2w₁w₂σ₁₂. Identities: E(αx)=αE(x), σ²(αx)=α²σ²(x), σ(αx)=|α|σ(x).

pages.title: Covariance and correlation
pages.summary: σ₁₂ = E[(r₁−E r₁)(r₂−E r₂)]; ρ₁₂ = σ₁₂/(σ₁σ₂) ∈ [−1,1]. ρ>0 co-movement; ρ=0 no linear co-movement (independence under joint normality); ρ<0 opposite moves.

pages.title: The principle of diversification
pages.summary: Equal-weighted two stocks, σ₁²=σ₂²=0.04: σ²_p = 0.02 + 0.02ρ₁₂. Table: ρ=+1→0.04 (no benefit); +0.5→0.03; 0→0.02 (halved); −0.5→0.01; −1→0 (risk eliminated). ρ<1 ⟹ portfolio variance below either stock alone.

pages.title: Variance of an N-asset portfolio
pages.summary: σ²_p = ΣΣ w_i w_j σ_ij = WᵀVW. N=100: 100 variances vs 9,900 covariances — covariance drives portfolio risk. Covariance of two portfolios σ_AB = W_AᵀVW_B. Beta of asset i with portfolio p: β_ip = Cov(r_i,R_p)/σ²(R_p).

pages.title: The basic allocation problem
pages.summary: Choosing among investments in mean/std-dev (E,S) space. Three cases: (1) one risky + riskless, (2) two risky, (3) many risky.

pages.title: Case 1 — One risky + one riskless asset
pages.summary: Feasible set is the straight Capital Allocation Line through rf and the risky asset. Example numbers: T-bills rf=5.5%, S&P E=7.9%, σ=12.1%; 50/50 point and 130% levered point marked. E[R_p]=wE[r]+(1−w)rf; σ_p = wσ.

pages.title: The slope of the CAL
pages.summary: Slope = (E[r_p]−rf)/σ_p — the Sharpe ratio, constant along the CAL. Utility over (E,σ) picks the point.

pages.title: The utility function
pages.summary: U(E,S) = E − αS². Increasing in E, decreasing in S. α = risk aversion; α=0 neutral, α<0 risk loving.

pages.title: Indifference curves
pages.summary: Loci of equal utility in (S,E) plane; higher curves = higher utility; optimum = highest curve tangent to feasible set. Figure with three parallel upward parabolas.

pages.title: Different investors have different indifference curves
pages.summary: Pension-fund manager (high α): steep curves, needs big E jump for small σ increase. Aggressive speculator (low α): flat curves. Figure with two curves crossing at a₁.

pages.title: Comparing portfolios — mean–variance dominance
pages.summary: i is MV-preferred to 1 if E_i ≥ E₁ and σ_i ≤ σ₁ with one strict. Quadrant figure: NW preferred, SE dominated, NE/SW ambiguous.

pages.title: Solving the optimization: one risky + one riskless
pages.summary: max_ω (1−ω)rf + ωE_P − αω²S_P². FOC: E_P − rf − 2αωS_P² = 0 ⟹ ω* = (E_P − rf)/(2αS_P²). Higher excess return → bigger position; higher variance or α → smaller.

pages.title: Case 2 — Two risky assets, feasible set bends with ρ
pages.summary: ρ=+1 straight line; +0.5 bows left; 0 more; −1 perfectly hedged riskless combination exists. σ²_p = w₁²σ₁² + w₂²σ₂² + 2w₁w₂ρ₁₂σ₁σ₂. Figure assets: (σ=18,E=6) and (σ=15,E=12).

pages.title: The investment opportunity set — stocks and bonds
pages.summary: S&P (σ=15,E=9), bonds (σ=8,E=4), ρ=0.2: w∈[0,1] traces a curve; leftmost point = MVP; sample 30/70 mix at (7.85, 5.5).

pages.title: Case 3 — Many risky assets: the feasible region
pages.summary: Feasible set fills a 2D bullet-shaped region; left boundary a hyperbola; leftmost point MVP; portion above MVP = efficient frontier; frontier dominates the interior. With rf, investor maximizes CAL slope (Sharpe).

pages.title: Case 3 — The efficient frontier is the upper half
pages.summary: Every portfolio above-MVP has a same-σ twin on the lower branch with lower return; only the upper branch is efficient. Figure highlights upper branch, dashed same-σ pair.

pages.title: Case 3 — The tangency portfolio: max-Sharpe on the frontier
pages.summary: Gold line from rf tangent to the upper branch = highest-Sharpe ray; tangency point T unique MV optimum among risky assets. Preview of two-fund separation: everyone holds T; only the T-vs-rf mix varies.

pages.title: Finding the optimal portfolio
pages.summary: Drag the indifference curve down to the CAL; first contact = optimum. Two equivalent approaches: utility (quadratic) or distributional (MVN ⟹ MV). Animated indifference-curve family.

pages.title: Setting up the optimization
pages.summary: Notation W, R, V, 1. min WᵀVW s.t. WᵀR = r_p, Wᵀ1 = 1. Two multipliers; closed-form W*; substitute back for the frontier equation.

pages.title: The Lagrangian and first-order condition
pages.summary: L = WᵀVW − λ₁(WᵀR−r_p) − λ₂(Wᵀ1−1). Gradient: 2VW = λ₁R + λ₂1 ⟹ W* = ½V⁻¹(λ₁R+λ₂1) = ½V⁻¹[R 1](λ₁,λ₂)ᵀ.

pages.title: Solving for the Lagrange multipliers
pages.summary: Pre-multiply by [R 1]ᵀ: (r_p,1)ᵀ = ½A(λ₁,λ₂)ᵀ with A=[R 1]ᵀV⁻¹[R 1]. Boxed: W* = V⁻¹[R 1]A⁻¹(r_p,1)ᵀ.

pages.title: The fundamental matrix A
pages.summary: A = [[a,b],[b,c]] with a=RᵀV⁻¹R, b=1ᵀV⁻¹R, c=1ᵀV⁻¹1. A⁻¹ = (1/(ac−b²))[[c,−b],[−b,a]]. Three scalars summarize the frontier.

pages.title: The equation of the efficient frontier
pages.summary: σ²_p = W*ᵀVW* collapses (A⁻¹AA⁻¹=A⁻¹) to σ²_p = (r_p,1)A⁻¹(r_p,1)ᵀ = (a − 2b·r_p + c·r_p²)/(ac−b²). Parabola in (σ², r); hyperbola in (σ, r).
formulas: sigma_p^2 = (a - 2 b r_p + c r_p^2)/(a c - b^2)

pages.title: The minimum-variance portfolio (MVP)
pages.summary: dσ²/dr = 0 ⟹ r_MVP = b/c; substituting back gives σ²_MVP = 1/c.

pages.title: A remarkable property of the MVP
pages.summary: W_MVP = V⁻¹1/(1ᵀV⁻¹1). Cov of ANY portfolio p with MVP: W_pᵀVW_MVP = (W_pᵀ1)/(1ᵀV⁻¹1) = 1/c = σ²_MVP — the same constant for all p.

pages.title: An equivalent characterization of the MVP
pages.summary: Perturb equal weights: R_p = R_EW + δr_i − δr_k; dσ²/dδ|₀ = 2σ_EW,i − 2σ_EW,k.

pages.title: The MVP is where these covariances all equalize
pages.summary: At a minimum no perturbation lowers variance ⟹ Cov(r_i, R_MVP) equal for all i. Diagnostic: equal covariances ⟹ candidate is the MVP.

pages.title: Two-fund separation
pages.summary: For any frontier P there is a zero-beta companion P_z: R = r_Pz·1 + (VW_P/σ²_P)(r_P − r_Pz). With rf: R = rf·1 + β(r_T − rf) — beta representation; expected excess return ∝ covariance with T. Foreshadows CAPM. Figure with T, T_z, P, P_z construction.

pages.title: MVP and tangency — in summary
pages.summary: W_MVP = V⁻¹1/(1ᵀV⁻¹1), equal-covariance property. W_T = V⁻¹(R−rf1)/(1ᵀV⁻¹(R−rf1)), max Sharpe, equal (E−rf)/Cov ratio property. Together they span the frontier.

pages.title: Portfolio optimization in practice — Jorion (FAJ 1992)
pages.summary: MV takes μ, V as known; both are estimated. Optimizer concentrates on high-μ̂ and attractive-covariance assets — the most error-prone inputs (double penalty). Constraints (no short sales, position limits, costs, tracking error) help. Jorion's answer: simulate.

pages.title: Jorion's illustration — global bond portfolios
pages.summary: 1978–88, 7 currency bond markets, no short sales. Frontier table: top point (avg 15.42, sd 17.31) puts 98% in Japanese Yen. Max return/risk row: 11.96/10.82 with 55% USD, 34% Yen. World index 11.31/10.94 diversified. Corner solutions, extreme bets.

pages.title: Problems with MV optimization in practice
pages.summary: Concentration on extreme estimates; sensitivity to covariance estimates; in-sample bias; a single realization of a random sample. Fix: run simulations.

pages.title: Simulations — the recipe
pages.summary: 1 assume distribution (MVN); 2 estimate μ, V from history; 3 draw sample of N returns T times; 4 re-estimate; 5 form optimal portfolio; 6 repeat 1,000–10,000×; 7 compare simulated vs estimated (estimated always wins in-sample by construction).

pages.title: Comparing actual and simulated weights
pages.summary: W*_T = V⁻¹R/(1ᵀV⁻¹R) from actual; W^S_T from simulated R^S, V^S. Compare W*ᵀR vs W^SᵀR and variances — apply simulated weights to ACTUAL parameters.

pages.title: The Gibbons–Ross–Shanken (1989) F-test
pages.summary: F = [T(T−N−1)/(N(T−2))]·(θ*² − θ_p²)/(1+θ_p²), θ = Sharpe ratio. Null: benchmark efficient ⟹ F ~ F(N, T−N−1). High F ⟹ unlikely efficient.

pages.title: More practical considerations
pages.summary: Out-of-sample possible. MVP easier to estimate than tangency: depends only on V (second moments have smaller sampling error than means). Relaxing short-sale constraints increases estimation error — flexibility vs stability trade-off.

pages.title: Statistically equivalent global bond portfolios
pages.summary: Cloud width = estimation risk. Figure A (no short sales): tight cloud, countries plot below. Figure C (short sales): much wider. Constraints keep the cloud tight at the cost of in-sample Sharpe.

pages.title: Jorion Figure A — simulated tangencies, no short sales
pages.summary: 500 simulated 10-year samples; each point a simulated tangency evaluated at true parameters. Cloud elongated along the frontier; bounded.

pages.title: Jorion Figure C — simulated tangencies, with short sales
pages.summary: Same exercise with short sales: dramatically wider cloud (some σ>23%, others ~9%). In-sample Sharpe rises, out-of-sample collapses.

pages.title: The fundamental question
pages.summary: Why do some securities earn higher average returns? Risk — but what is risk, and what premium does it command? CAPM answers both. Applications: valuation, fund evaluation, event studies, efficiency tests.

pages.title: The separation principle
pages.summary: With rf, everyone's optimal risky portfolio is the tangency regardless of risk aversion; investors differ only in the T-vs-rf mix (lend or lever). Without rf, optimum sits on the frontier.

pages.title: Identifying the tangency portfolio
pages.summary: Defining property: (E[r_i]−rf)/Cov(r_i,R_T) equal across all assets. W_T = V⁻¹(R−rf1)/(1ᵀV⁻¹(R−rf1)). Same reward-to-risk ratio at the margin.

pages.title: From tangency portfolio to the CAPM equation
pages.summary: Apply the property to T itself: (E[r_i]−rf)/Cov(r_i,R_T) = (E[R_T]−rf)/Var(R_T). Rearranged: E[r_i] = rf + [Cov/Var](E[R_T]−rf). Marginal, not average, contribution to risk sets required return.

pages.title: Beta and the CAPM equation
pages.summary: β_i = Cov(r_i,R_T)/Var(R_T) — regression slope. E[r_i] = rf + β_i(E[R_T]−rf). Equilibrium: everyone holds T, supply = demand ⟹ T is the market portfolio. Boxed CAPM: E[r_i] = rf + β_i(E[R_M]−rf).

pages.title: Why do we hold the market portfolio?
pages.summary: Assumptions: MVN returns, everyone uses MV, homogeneous beliefs, risk-free borrowing/lending. Then all hold T; T=M; CAL becomes the Capital Market Line; risk that matters = covariance with M.

pages.title: The CAPM — summary
pages.summary: E[r_i] = rf + β_i(E[R_M]−rf), β_i = Cov/σ²_M. Assumptions recap. Applications: cost of capital and valuation, fund/manager evaluation, event studies, mispricing and efficiency tests.
